Notes on a Forgotten Compiler

In a filing cabinet in Trondheim there is a magnetic tape labelled simply “K-2, do not optimise”. It contains the only surviving copy of a compiler that, for eleven months in 1987, was the fastest path from source to silicon in northern Europe — and the story of why nobody used it twice.

The K-2 made one promise: it would never allocate memory it could not prove it would free. The proof engine was nine hundred lines of hand-written Prolog. The error messages were in Norwegian, in verse.

Its author, who still answers email but only on Tuesdays, maintains that the design was correct and the world was early. Modern borrow checkers, he points out, rhyme too — just less deliberately.

What remains useful is the test suite: four hundred programs, each a tiny fable about ownership. Port them to any new language and you learn where its sympathies lie. Rust passes three hundred and ninety-one. C passes all four hundred, which the author considers the strongest argument against C ever produced.

The tape itself has never been read back. The drive that could read it was scrapped in 1994, and the museum that owns the cabinet insists this is now a conservation issue rather than an engineering one.
